newsitem.title: UK: Base metals ease from highs, gold firmer in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: Base metals ease from highs, gold firmer in quiet trade.

text.p: Base metals eased back under profittaking from the higher levels reached early Friday on speculative buying while gold and other precious metals ended higher but lacked definite direction. Three-month copper prices peaked at $2,175, but eased back when they failed to breach this resistance point, ending slightly weaker at the kerb close at $2,150, down $5.
The market, however, still looked in tight supply with the premium of nearby delivery over three months forward metal firming about $4 to $110.
The fact that the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) daily average output in November rose to 51,700 tonnes, compared with 51,100 in October knocked aluminium.
It tried higher levels but pulled back from a peak of $1,566, failing to confront resistance of $1,570. Aluminium closed at $1,546 on Thursday.

An optimistic outlook for base metals came from broker Rudolf Wolff in a report on Friday that said prices seemed to be gathering steam for another rally like the one from 1993 to 1995, when prices gained 102 percent on average. "Many of the metals are facing a supply/demand deficit in 1997 and 1988, and considering the trade have been destocking in 1996, an improvement in the order flow of semi-fabricated products should be quickly reflected in higher demand for metal," said the report.
Gold was firmer at $369.10/369.60 against $368.80/369.30 on Thursday and dealers said the market was very quiet ahead of next week's Christmas holiday.
"There is absolutely nothing happening, just professionals trading the range," one dealer.
Another dealer said "We are just seeing the professionals playing the range. The funds and the producers have gone on holiday already."
Dealers said there was no direction offered overnight from Tokyo and Hong Kong which closed very slightly firmer and unchanged respectively.

In other commodity markets, statistician F.O. Licht said on Friday that world coffee production should reach 97.7 million bags in 1996/97, sharply up on the 1995/96 figure of 87.7 million bags. Licht said the increase was largerly due to a recovery in Brazil's crop.
Fear of frost in Mexico's coffee-growing areas diminished after growers said the areas escaped sub-zero temperatures in the early hours of Friday morning.
In oil, news that Iraq had signed more oil sale contracts under the United Nation's oil-for-food exchange made little impact on the market.
Some 20 companies have now confirmed agreements with Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation for a combined 530,000 barrels per day (bpd) of purchases.
Iraq's first exports in six years of U.N. sanctions set sail last Monday.
